verdict.failure_analysis:
Trial 2 failed incomplete-token-after-closed-list because it treated trailing incomplete markup after as a failed scan of the first list. The specific misconception was loop ordering: it filtered out closers with continue before checking get_current_depth() < $list_depth, so it missed the UL closer, kept scanning, then saw paused_at_incomplete_token(). The relevant docs did contain the rule under WP_HTML_Processor::next_token() ('does not stop when the element matched by an earlier next_tag() call ends') and get_current_depth() ('first token to report a depth less than N is the element's own closing token'), but the direct-child recipe showed only the child predicate and did not explicitly warn that subtree-exit checks must happen before closer/type filters. Trial 2 failed unsupported-after-closed-list for the same boundary misconception. It skipped the closed-list boundary, scanned into later unsupported
markup, observed get_last_error() === 'unsupported', and returned the original HTML. The docs' HTML Support/get_last_error sections explain that the processor aborts when unsupported markup is encountered, and the region-scan recipe says to check get_last_error() after the scan. The missing nuance is that for a mutation scoped to a bounded subtree, 'after the scan' means after the bounded subtree walk, not after draining the rest of the fragment. The docs worked well overall on processor choice and safe mutation patterns: all trials used WP_HTML_Processor rather than the Tag Processor, all avoided undocumented methods, and two trials followed the bookmark/depth/incomplete/error/get_updated_html pattern successfully.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three passed 8/8, with no errors, trigger errors, or `_doing_it_wrong` records. The docs appear to have successfully taught the key distinctions for this task: use the HTML Processor rather than the Tag Processor when document structure matters; use `create_fragment()` for body fragments; use `next_token()` when text nodes matter; bound subtree walks with `get_current_depth() >= recorded_depth`; gather ordinary DOM-style text only from `#text` tokens; and use `get_modifiable_text()` for already-decoded text. The strongest passages were `Which processor should I use?`, `Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree`, `next_token()`, and `get_current_depth()`. Near-misses were mostly harmless: trial 2 over-engineered implicit closer handling, trial 3 had unreachable text code, and all trials left the completion policy for unsupported or incomplete input implicit rather than checking `paused_at_incomplete_token()` / `get_last_error()`.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs state that closers are emitted for implicit and end-of-input closes, but they do not make optional-end-tag sibling transitions especially concrete. Trial 2 added redundant flushing on new openers, suggesting uncertainty about whether virtual closers are sufficient.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general note that optional-end-tag elements such as repeated sibling regions emit a closing token at the point the HTML parser closes the previous element, so a single closer-driven state machine can record empty and malformed-but-browser-valid regions without guessing from the next opener.

doc_gaps.problem: The inherited `get_tag()` documentation is valid, but the example is Tag Processor oriented and does not clearly spell out how `get_tag()` behaves during HTML Processor `next_token()` walks, especially for virtual tag tokens versus non-tag tokens.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that on HTML Processor tag tokens, including virtual tokens, `get_tag()` returns the uppercase element name and `get_token_name()` returns the same tag name; on non-tag tokens `get_tag()` returns null while `get_token_name()` returns names such as `#text`.

doc_gaps.problem: Completion policy for read-only extraction is described, but it is scattered across recipes. All trials returned best-effort results without explicitly deciding whether incomplete input or unsupported markup should be rejected.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a compact read-only extraction policy note: accumulated visited tokens remain usable; best-effort extractors may return them; strict extractors should check both `paused_at_incomplete_token()` and `get_last_error()` after the scan, with `get_last_error()` indicating parser abort rather than mere trailing truncation.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 8 hidden cases. The docs did well in four places: the Tag Processor “Which processor should I use?” section steered subjects away from flat tag/attribute editing and toward WP_HTML_Processor for normalized output and missing/implied closers; the HTML Processor “Recipe: rewrite while serializing tokens” and serialize_token() entry gave the exact mental model for building an output string while walking tokens; get_modifiable_text() clearly said decoded text is returned for #text tokens and warned that it is not a predicate for ordinary text; and the ordinary subtree text guidance made comments, attributes, SCRIPT/STYLE/TEXTAREA/TITLE opener-carried text, and split text nodes hard to confuse with wrappable DOM text. verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all 18 trial-case executions passed, and there were no _doing_it_wrong records. The docs succeeded because the Tag Processor overview clearly assigns flat, position-based class edits to WP_HTML_Tag_Processor; next_tag documents case-insensitive real-tag matching and excludes comments/raw text/incomplete tokens; add_class documents appending to existing classes; get_updated_html is documented as the right output method after queued edits; and the set_bookmark docs explicitly describe re-setting one name as the idiom for remembering the last matching tag. Near-miss: trial-1 chose WP_HTML_Processor and create_full_parser first. The docs do warn that create_fragment is usually more appropriate for chunks and that the lighter Tag Processor suffices for flat class edits, but a model can still over-read 'document or fragment' as a reason to use the structured processor. That did not fail the frozen cases, but it is less robust: if WP_HTML_Processor aborts on unsupported markup before a later H2, a bookmark-based scan may be incomplete unless get_last_error is checked or the Tag Processor is used instead.

doc_gaps.problem: A mixed contract like 'document or fragment' can lead readers to try create_full_parser first even when the operation is only a flat tag/class edit.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a decision note: for byte-preserving tag, attribute, or class edits, use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for both complete documents and fragments; choose create_full_parser only when full-document structural parsing, HEAD/doctype handling, or normalized serialization is required.

doc_gaps.problem: The Processor bookmark section omits the Tag Processor's explicit statement that setting an existing bookmark name moves it, which is the key contract behind 'last occurrence' scans.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial. The docs succeeded because the Tag Processor overview explicitly presents it as the tool for finding tags and changing attributes/classes, while the HTML Processor overview says Tag Processor is valuable for modifying attributes on individual tags. The Tag Processor workflow shows construction with new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor($html), next_tag() traversal, attribute edits, and get_updated_html(). The get_attribute_names_with_prefix() section provided the key contract: lowercase names, case-insensitive matching, and an uppercase DATA-* example. The next_tag() section also protected the comments case by saying only real HTML tags match and tag-like text inside comments/raw text is never modified. get_updated_html() clearly states it is the way to read queued edits while preserving untouched bytes. Near misses were minor: the prefix-name return contract does not explicitly say matched tags with no matching attributes return array(), and remove_attribute() is terse compared with the source behavior around case-insensitive names and duplicate attributes.

doc_gaps.problem: The rendered docs say the method returns array|null and null when no tag opener is matched, but they do not explicitly distinguish the matched-opener/no-matching-attributes case.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State that a matched tag opener with no matching attributes returns an empty array, while null means the processor is not currently matched on a tag opener.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say matching is case-insensitive and names are lowercase, but the practical implication is easy to miss: returned names are canonical names safe to pass back into attribute APIs.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence that returned lowercase names may be passed directly to get_attribute(), set_attribute(), or remove_attribute() while still targeting source attributes case-insensitively.

doc_gaps.problem: The method section only says it removes an attribute and returns whether one was removed. It omits important public behavior visible in source: matching is ASCII case-insensitive, false is returned when not on a tag opener or when the attribute was absent, and duplicate attributes with the same normalized name are removed too.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Expand the public contract with those behaviors, especially the case-insensitive name matching and the safe no-op behavior outside a matched opener or for absent attributes.

trials.notes: Used the right class (`WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()`), documented methods only, and the intended token-serialization pattern: walk with `next_token()`, skip `SPAN` tokens, append `serialize_token()`. Minor deduction: on processor creation failure or parser error it returns raw input, which the docs warn is neither normalized nor the accumulated rewrite.

verdict.failure_analysis:
Only trial-2 failed hidden cases. The common misconception was interpreting “remove every element” as “skip the whole subtree rooted at that element.” In `simple`, `attributes-discarded`, `adjacent-spans`, and `span-with-block-content`, the candidate skipped text, inline tags, and void tags that were descendants of `SPAN`, producing empty or content-missing output. In `nested-spans`, the depth counter amplified the same mistake by suppressing all nested contents. In `unclosed-span`, the HTML Processor did provide a virtual closing token as documented, but the candidate kept suppressing contents until that virtual closer, so the text before end-of-input was deleted.

The relevant documentation did include the key pattern under `html-processor.md` / `serialize_token()`: walking every token and concatenating `serialize_token()` reconstructs normalized HTML, and the example “Remove every SUP element but keep its contents” skips only matching tag tokens. That passage should have been enough for trials 1 and 3. The doc weakness is that nearby wording like “skip tokens to remove them” and the separate depth/subtree recipes do not explicitly contrast unwrapping a wrapper with pruning an element subtree. Trial-2 appears to combine those two ideas incorrectly.

doc_gaps.problem: The section gives a correct wrapper-removal example, but it does not explicitly distinguish “unwrap an element” from “remove an element and all descendants.” The phrase “skip tokens to remove them” can be overgeneralized into depth-based subtree skipping.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short contrast: to unwrap an element, skip only that element’s opener and closer tokens and continue serializing descendants; to prune a subtree, record depth or breadcrumbs and skip descendants until the boundary.

doc_gaps.problem: Depth-based walking is documented for subtree scans, but there is no warning that using an `inside_target` flag to gate serializer output will delete descendants.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a serializer-specific caution near the depth examples: depth bounds are for scanning or subtree pruning; for wrapper removal, child text and child elements remain later tokens and should still be serialized.

doc_gaps.problem: The overview says future support may include “Unwrapping a tag by removing its parent,” which can imply unwrapping is not currently possible, even though token serialization can perform stream-level wrapper removal.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that high-level node-editing helpers are future work, but token-by-token serialization can already implement filters such as dropping selected start/end tag tokens while preserving their contents.

doc_gaps.problem: Candidates used raw input or `normalize( $html )` as error fallbacks after a rewrite. The docs explain the consequences, but examples for string-returning rewrites do not show a normalized-output contract with a concrete fallback policy.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general string-returning rewrite example that chooses and names a fallback policy, emphasizing that raw input and `normalize( $html )` discard token-loop edits and may violate contracts requiring rewritten normalized output.
